messages.author: 2404274725ee6339
messages.subject: guidance for the generic model
parts:
Hi all,

I'm trying to benchmark the speed of R-INLA to use it as a baseline for a method we are developing, but I'm having trouble implementing it.

I have observations in 2D, and I am trying to fit a GMRF with a Matern kernel.

My plan is:
  • Use the finite differences method to discretize the field into a regular grid, and compute the sparse prior precision matrix. This is implemented in Python, and will be shared between the various methods in the benchmark. It saves the sparse matrix to disk.
  • Load the sparse precision matrix in R
  • Use the "generic" model and specify the precision matrix using the Cmatrix parameter
I couldn't find any guidance for using the generic model, but I tried the following:
precision <- readMM("prior_precision.mtx")
data <- read.csv("data.csv")
log_precision <- log(precision)
formula <- y ~ f(x, model = "generic", Cmatrix = log_precision)
inla(formula, data = data)

data.csv contains a column x which gives the row/column of the precision matrix that the data point corresponds to, and a column y which gives the observation value.

The above code crashes:
inla.mkl: src/inla.c:37061: inla_INLA_preopt_experimental: Assertion `ABS(res[1] - res[3]) < DMAX(1, ABS(res[1])) * 1e-6' failed.

My questions are:
  • Is this a sensible way of including R-INLA in the benchmark? Would R-INLA be faster if I performed the finite difference approximation in R-INLA, rather than passing in the sparse prior matrix?
  • Do you have any pointers for how to write the R-INLA portion of the code? Is the generic model the correct thing to use, and are their any examples of using it?

Many thanks for you help!

Oscar
https://oscarkey.github.io/

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] guidance for the generic model
parts:
I think the error you show is caused by something else. make sure you
have the most recent testing version 23.09.09

in the formula, then 'x' should be 'x=i + (j-1)*nrow' for which '(i,j)'
is observed. inla() only understand one-dimensional indexing.

easiest is to use a square region where nrow=ncol ;-)

benchmarking is always difficult. make sure to have some size from
nrow,ncol otherwise you only measure the time-to-do-nothing, which is
actually something.

> inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=NA))$cpu
Pre Running Post Total
0.3656902313 0.3125338554 0.0540266037 0.7322506905


please note that this measure the time from within R, while actually
most of the time is R doing admin, as the C-program report this

> r=inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=NA))
> i=grep("Preparations", r$logfile)
> r$logfile[i:(i+6)]
[1] " Preparations : 0.012 seconds"
[2] " Approx inference (stage1): 0.045 seconds"
[3] " Approx inference (stage2): 0.000 seconds"
[4] " Approx inference (total) : 0.045 seconds"
[5] " Output : 0.001 seconds"
[6] " ------------------------------------------"
[7] " Total : 0.057 seconds"

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] guidance for the generic model
parts:
Apart from the general difficulty of benchmarking, the code is
strangely written:

> log_precision <- log(precision)
> formula <- y ~ f(x, model = "generic", Cmatrix = log_precision)

Cmatrix should be the precision matrix, and presumably your
"precision" is that matrix, so it's not clear what you're trying to do
here.
I think you're looking for "generic0", documented in
INLA::inla.doc("generic0"), that by default has a scaling parameter
that's estimated. You can set that to a fixed value if you're not
estimating it, with f(..., hyper=list(prec=list(initial=log(1),
fixed=TRUE)))
but then if your model only has this component, there isn't anything
for inla to do except compute the kriging means and variances, and the
timings will mostly be overhead costs.

Finn

parts: Thank you for the quick response! The combination of using the generic0 model and the correct indexing fixed the problem. And thank you for the tip on how to access the timing report from the C program.

> if your model only has this component, there isn't anything
> for inla to do except compute the kriging means and variances, and the
> timings will mostly be overhead costs.

We're actually using R-INLA as a baseline for computing kringing means and variances. We're considering large fields, e.g. 8 million points, at which scale we're hoping the computation will dominate the time rather than overhead costs. Of course, let me know if you don't think this is a sensible thing to do.

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] guidance for the generic model
parts:
Hi,

if that's all you're using it for, I suspect calling inla.qsolve() and
inla.qinv() might be preferable. It still involves writing the matrix
to disk (internally in the inla code), but it skips everything else.
You just need to construct the conditional precision matrix; Q_cond =
Q_x + A' Q_e A, where the observation model was y = A x + e, with e ~
N(0, Q_e^-1).
diag(inla.qinv(Q_cond)) will give you the conditional marginal
variances. inla.qsolve(Q_cond,
the_RHS_of_the_precision_kriging_equations) gives you the kriging
mean.

Finn

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] guidance for the generic model
parts:
these implementations are mainly to access the same internals as the
inla-program, hence there is quite some overhead as R write to file,
starts program as a separate process who read file, do comp, write to
file, then R reads file. 

like

> a=Sys.time(); inla.qinv(matrix(1,1,1)); Sys.time()-a
1 x 1 sparse Matrix of class "dgTMatrix"

[1,] 1
Time difference of 0.327085495 secs
>

which is time taken for doing nothing. so its reasonable to subtract
this constant from timings and similar with inla.qsolve().

well, it seems like you want to time sparse-factorisations, and not INLA
itself... as Finn says, just be clear in your writing.

Best
Havard
